items.sentence_raw: Information theory lies at the heart of everything - from DVD players and the genetic code of DNA to the physics of the universe at its most fundamental.
It has been central to the development of the science of communication, which enables data to be sent electronically and has therefore had a major impact on our lives.
In April 2002 an event took place which demonstrated one of the many applications of information theory.
items.explain: Q31: The question asks for a **detailed account of an incident**. The passage starts with *'In April 2002 an event took place'* and then tells the whole story of fixing the Voyager probe — this is a **detailed incident**. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: The space probe Voyager I, launched in 1977, had sent back spectacular images of Jupiter and Saturn and then soared out of the Solar System on a one-way mission to the stars.
items.explain:
Q33: The passage says the probe sent back *'spectacular images of Jupiter and Saturn'*. So the answers are **Jupiter** and **Saturn**.

Q34: The passage says the probe *'soared out of the Solar System'*. So the answer is **Solar System**.

items.sentence_raw: After 25 years of exposure to the freezing temperatures of deep space, the probe was beginning to show its age.
Sensors and circuits were on the brink of failing and NASA experts realized that they had to do something or lose contact with their probe forever.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says *'Sensors and circuits were on the brink of failing'* — **'on the brink of failing'** means they were about to stop working. So the answers are **sensors** and **circuits**.

items.sentence_raw: The solution was to get a message to Voyager I to instruct it to use spares to change the failing parts.
items.explain: Q36: The passage says the message told the probe *'to use spares to change the failing parts'*. So the answer is **spares**.

items.sentence_raw: With the probe 12 billion kilometers from Earth, this was not an easy task.
By means of a radio dish belonging to NASA's Deep Space Network, the message was sent out into the depths of space.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says the message was sent *'By means of a radio dish'*. So the answer is **radio dish**.

items.sentence_raw: Even travelling at the speed of light, it took over 11 hours to reach its target, far beyond the orbit of Pluto.
Yet, incredibly, the little probe managed to hear the faint call from its home planet and successfully made the switchover.
It was the longest-distance repair job history, and a triumph for the NASA engineers.
But it also highlighted the astonishing power of the techniques developed by American communications engineer Claude Shannon, who had died just a year earlier.
Born in 1916 in Petoskey, Michigan, Shannon showed an early talent for maths and for building gadgets, and made breakthroughs in the foundations of computer technology when still a student.
While at Bell Laboratories, Shannon developed information theory, but shunned the resulting acclaim.
items.explain: Q29: The question asks about Shannon's **attitude to fame**. The passage says he *'shunned the resulting acclaim'* — **'shunned'** means he avoided it, and **'acclaim'** means **'fame'**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: In the 1940s, he single-handedly created an entire science of communication which has since inveigled its way into a host of applications, from DVDs to satellite communications to bar codes - any area, in short, where data has to be conveyed rapidly yet accurately.

This all seems light years away from the down-to-earth uses Shannon originally had for his work, which began when he was a 22-year-old graduate engineering student at the prestigious Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1939.
He set out with an apparently simple aim: to pin down the precise meaning of the concept of 'information'.
items.explain: Q32: The question asks what Shannon **initially intended to achieve**. The passage says *'He set out with an apparently simple aim: to pin down the precise meaning of the concept of 'information'.'* — **'set out with an aim'** means **'initially intended to achieve'**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: The most basic form of information, Shannon argued, is whether something is true or false - which can be captured in the binary unit, or 'bit', of the form 1 or 0.
items.explain: Q38: The passage says Shannon's most basic form of information is *'whether something is true or false'* — this was his **starting point**. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: Having identified this fundamental unit, Shannon set about defining otherwise vague ideas about information and how to transmit it from place to place.
In the process he discovered something surprising: it is always possible to guarantee information will get through random interference - 'noise' - intact.
Noise usually means unwanted sounds which interfere with genuine information.
Information theory generalises this idea via theorems that capture the effects of noise with mathematical precision.
In particular, Shannon showed that noise sets a limit on the rate at which information can pass along communication channels while remaining error-free.
items.explain: Q27: The question asks about **factors** that affect sending information. The passage says *'This rate depends on the relative strengths of the signal and noise'* and the channel's *'capacity'* — these are the **factors**. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: This rate depends on the relative strengths of the signal and noise travelling down the communication channel, and on its capacity (its 'bandwidth').
items.explain:
Q27: The question asks about **factors** that affect sending information. The passage says *'This rate depends on the relative strengths of the signal and noise'* and the channel's *'capacity'* — these are the **factors**. So the answer is **D**.

Q39: The passage says the rate *'depends on the relative strengths of the signal and noise'* and the *'absolute maximum rate'* is *'given signal strength and noise level'*. This matches the question exactly. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: The resulting limit, given in units of bits per second, is the absolute maximum rate of error-free communication given signal strength and noise level.
items.explain: Q39: The passage says the rate *'depends on the relative strengths of the signal and noise'* and the *'absolute maximum rate'* is *'given signal strength and noise level'*. This matches the question exactly. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: The trick, Shannon showed, is to find ways of packaging up - 'coding' - information to cope with the ravages of noise, while staying within the information-carrying capacity - 'bandwidth' - of the communication system being used.
Over the years scientists have devised many such coding methods, and they have proved crucial in many technological feats.

The Voyager spacecraft transmitted data using codes which added one extra bit for every single bit of information; the result was an error rate of just one bit in 10,000-and stunningly clear pictures of the planets.

Other codes have become part of everyday life - such as the Universal Product Code, or bar code, which uses a simple error-detecting system that ensures supermarket check-out lasers can read the price even on, say, a crumpled bag of crisps.
items.explain: Q30: The question asks for a **machine** that reads **incomplete information**. The passage describes a bar code system where a laser reads a price *'even on, say, a crumpled bag of crisps'* — a crumpled bag gives **incomplete information**. So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: As recently as 1993, engineers made a major breakthrough by discovering so-called turbo codes - which come very close to Shannon's ultimate limit for the maximum rate that data can be transmitted reliably, and now play a key role in the mobile videophone revolution.
items.explain: Q40: The question says products now **exceed** Shannon's limit. But the passage says turbo codes *'come very close to Shannon's ultimate limit'* — ***'very close to' does NOT mean 'more than'***. They have not passed the limit. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Shannon also laid the foundations of more efficient ways of storing information, by stripping out superfluous ('redundant') bits from data which contributed little real information.
items.explain: Q28: The question asks about leaving out **unnecessary information**. The passage says Shannon found ways to store information by *'stripping out superfluous ('redundant') bits'* — **'superfluous'** means **'unnecessary'**. So the answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: As mobile phone text messages like 'I CN C U' show, it is often possible to leave out a lot of data without losing much meaning.
As with error correction, however, there's a limit beyond which messages become too ambiguous.
Shannon showed how to calculate this limit, opening the way to the design of compression methods that cram maximum information into the minimum space.
